title: Fire hoses on the City Hall stairs

place.label: San Francisco City Hall rotunda, 1 Dr Carlton B Goodlett Pl

hook: Students sang 'We Shall Not Be Moved' outside a Red-hunting hearing. Police answered with fire hoses, and a decade of protest was born on a marble staircase.
story: In May 1960 the House Un-American Activities Committee came to City Hall to question suspected Communists, including union leaders and teachers. On Friday, May 13, it let mostly its own supporters into the hearing. Students from Bay Area campuses sat down outside the chamber, chanting and singing 'We Shall Not Be Moved' [1]. Then, without warning, police turned fire hoses on them. The protesters held on at the top of the rotunda staircase 'like trees in a hurricane', the Chronicle reported, until they were washed down the marble steps while officers swung clubs [1]. 'If you know what water and marble is like, it's like glass,' recalled Becky Jenkins, then a 23-year-old San Francisco State student [1][2]. Sixty-four people were arrested. Charges against all but one were dropped, and he was acquitted [1][2]. The next day longshoremen from the ILWU joined a much bigger crowd outside [2]. HUAC's film 'Operation Abolition' blamed Communists, but on television the soaked demonstrators looked like college kids [1]. Veterans of 'Black Friday' later said it led straight to Berkeley's Free Speech Movement [1].

title: A cup of coffee starts a riot

place.label: Site of Gene Compton's Cafeteria, 101 Taylor St at Turk

hook: Three years before Stonewall, trans women at an all-night Tenderloin cafeteria fought back against police. For decades almost nobody remembered it happened.
story: Gene Compton's cafeteria at Turk and Taylor was open all night, and in the 1960s it was a haven for drag queens, trans women and young hustlers who spent hours over cheap coffee. Management often called the police to clear them out. Officers arrested people for 'female impersonation' [1]. On an August night in 1966, an officer grabbed a queen and she threw her coffee in his face. The cafeteria 'erupted', historian Susan Stryker says. Sugar shakers went through the windows, heavy purses swung at police, a patrol car was trashed and a newsstand burned [1][3]. 'We just got tired of it,' Amanda St. Jaymes later said. 'We wanted our rights' [1]. The riot made no newspapers, and the exact date has never been found [2]. The only written record that survived was a short piece by activist Raymond Broshears in the program for the city's first Pride parade in 1972 [1]. Stryker pieced the story back together from archives and interviews for her 2005 documentary 'Screaming Queens' [2]. In 2021, photos of a 1970 hotel fire turned up on Facebook showing Compton's sign in the background, one of the few known pictures of its exterior [3].

title: The pastor who took down the cross

place.label: Glide Memorial Church, 330 Ellis St at Taylor

hook: When Cecil Williams arrived, Glide's congregation was down to a handful. He opened the doors to addicts, sex workers and gay runaways, and it grew into a phenomenon.
story: In 1962 Glide Memorial, a well-endowed Methodist church at Ellis and Taylor, hired the Rev. Lewis Durham to rethink its mission. Durham brought in young clergy, among them Cecil Williams, the grandson of a slave from segregated San Angelo, Texas, who arrived in 1963 [1][2]. Randy Shaw, who wrote a history of the neighbourhood, says the congregation was 'almost down to the single digits' [2]. Williams rebuilt it by becoming a fierce advocate for civil rights and, most controversially then, for gay and transgender people at a time when police were arresting them in bars [2]. Glide's pastors worked with sex workers, runaways, hippies and addicts. In the early 1970s an activist said: 'You knew where the women's movement was: it was at Glide church at 7:30' [1]. Williams took the crucifix out of the sanctuary. A 1995 Chronicle profile dates this to 1965, while other accounts say 1967 [3]. Sunday services, with a gospel choir and jazz band, became joyous celebrations [2][3]. In 1980 Glide started a free meals programme serving three hot meals a day [2]. Williams stepped down as pastor in 2000 and died in 2024, aged 94 [2].

title: Where American Beauty was recorded

place.label: Wally Heider Studios (now Hyde Street Studios), 245 Hyde St

hook: Behind a plain door in a former film warehouse, the Grateful Dead, CSNY and Creedence cut classics. A drunk Grace Slick warned the night receptionist not to wake her.
story: In 1969 Los Angeles engineer Wally Heider leased 245 Hyde Street, a building 20th Century Fox had used to store film, and built what is generally considered the Bay Area's first high-tech recording studio [1]. Unusually, it gave musicians almost complete creative control [1]. 'It was ground zero,' engineer Stephen Barncard said. 'San Francisco for years had been waiting for a full-fledged professional studio' [2]. Here the Grateful Dead recorded 'American Beauty', Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young made 'Déjà Vu', and Creedence Clearwater Revival cut 'Cosmo's Factory' [1]. Jefferson Airplane, Santana, Van Morrison and Herbie Hancock worked here too [1][2]. In 1974 Susie Foot, 28, was the studio's gopher, guarding the front desk at night. Grace Slick wandered out of a Jefferson Starship session and told her: 'My name's Grace, and I drink a lot. If you see me passed out on the couch, don't wake me up' [1]. Foot rose to first engineer by the time Heider's closed in 1980 [1]. Under Michael Ward it reopened as Hyde Street Studios, where Tupac Shakur, Green Day and Cake recorded. A sidewalk plaque now marks the spot [1][3].

title: The Mitchell Brothers' 'Carnegie Hall'

place.label: Mitchell Brothers O'Farrell Theatre, 895 O'Farrell St

hook: Two film-school brothers opened a porn theatre on the Fourth of July, beat the city in court over and over, and ended in a Marin County shooting.
story: Jim and Artie Mitchell got their start in San Francisco State's film department, then opened their theatre at 895 O'Farrell Street on July 4, 1969 [1]. Police raided it again and again, but prosecutors struggled to win convictions [1]. The brothers were involved in nearly 200 obscenity lawsuits, and their wins helped set legal precedents far beyond the city [2]. In 1972 they spent $60,000 on 'Behind the Green Door'. Just before release, their star Marilyn Chambers told them her face would soon be on Ivory soap boxes nationwide. The publicity made it a smash, and it went on to earn over $50 million [1][2]. After a 1980 vice raid, the brothers put Mayor Dianne Feinstein's phone number on their marquee under 'For a Good Time Call…' [2]. Hunter S. Thompson dubbed the club the 'Carnegie Hall' of sex in America [1][2]. The story turned dark on February 27, 1991, when Jim shot Artie dead at Artie's Corte Madera home. Jim was convicted of voluntary manslaughter [1][2]. The theatre survived him but not the pandemic, closing for good in 2020 [2].

title: A bordello becomes a jazz jewel box

place.label: Great American Music Hall, 859 O'Farrell St

hook: Built for a blind political boss's pleasure palace, nearly lost, it was reborn in 1972. Duke Ellington got his own shower. The Grateful Dead brought live crickets.
story: 859 O'Farrell opened in 1907 as Blanco's, a lavish cafe of gilded mirrors and frescoes. By mid-century it had passed through Sally Rand's cabaret, a Moose lodge and a restaurant whose owner vanished amid a tax investigation, after which the building was sold at an IRS auction. It was in such decline that it nearly came down [1][2]. In 1972 Tom Bradshaw bought it, restored it and renamed it the Great American Music Hall [2]. It started as a jazz room. Sarah Vaughan, Bill Evans and Duke Ellington played here, and Ellington had a dressing room and shower built in the basement for his 1970s residencies. Carmen McRae and Sonny Rollins recorded live albums on its stage [1]. In February 1974 Journey debuted here with drummer Aynsley Dunbar [1]. The Grateful Dead recorded 'One From the Vault' at an invitation-only show in 1975 [1][2]. According to the hall's general manager, they wanted to open with the sound of crickets and brought in live ones. It was too dark and cold for the crickets to chirp, so the band used a tape, and crickets roamed the building for ages [1]. The 1989 Loma Prieta quake shook loose a long-papered-over secret door to the hotel next door [1].

title: Twenty-five days inside the Federal Building

place.label: Former Federal Building (HEW offices), 50 United Nations Plaza

hook: Disabled activists moved into a federal office and refused to leave. The Black Panthers brought dinner every night. They walked out with a civil-rights law.
story: Section 504 of the 1973 Rehabilitation Act banned discrimination against disabled people in federally funded programmes, but it could not take effect until the Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare signed its rules. Four years later he still had not [1]. On April 5, 1977, after a rally in Civic Center, more than 100 people, many of them disabled, entered HEW's regional offices on the fourth floor of 50 United Nations Plaza and stayed [1][2]. Organizers Judy Heumann and Kitty Cone had spent years building alliances, and it showed [2]. Officials turned off the hot water and cut the phones down to a pair of pay phones [1]. Glide Memorial, Delancey Street and above all the Black Panther Party, which brought hot meals every day for fellow Panther Brad Lomax and the others, kept the sit-in fed [1][2]. Congressmen held a hearing inside, and Mayor Moscone brought in portable showers [1]. On April 28 Joseph Califano signed the regulations unchanged. Two days later the occupiers walked out together to champagne on UN Plaza [1]. It was the longest occupation of a federal building in US history. Accounts put it at 25 or 26 days [1][2].

title: Leroy Looper saves the Cadillac Hotel

place.label: Cadillac Hotel, 380 Eddy St at Leavenworth

hook: A 180-room hotel had 40 tenants and a drug market out front. A former Harlem street kid bought it with no money down and pioneered a new kind of housing.
story: The Cadillac Hotel went up after the 1906 earthquake, a grand place where guests checked their furs at the front desk [1]. By the 1960s it was on the way down. One owner, a then-unknown Donald Fisher, before he founded the Gap, stripped much of its ornament [1]. In July 1977 it was sold, with no money down, to Leroy Looper, who ran the Reality House West drug-treatment programme [1][2]. The 180-room hotel had only 40 tenants. Looper planned to restore it and house people coming out of prison. The mostly elderly residents were wary, so he promised they could vote to end the halfway-house programme if they were unhappy. They never did [1]. The legendary manager Sarah Kearney swept the sidewalk daily and used her broom on anyone dealing drugs in front of the hotel [1]. Randy Shaw calls it the West Coast's first 'supportive housing', and its lobby became a meeting hall for neighbourhood organizing [1][2]. Reality House West was the first group to blaze the Tenderloin's nonprofit-housing trail [2]. Today the Tenderloin Museum occupies its corner at 398 Eddy [3].

title: The neighbourhood that stopped the towers

place.label: Eastern edge of the Tenderloin near Mason and O'Farrell Sts

hook: Three hotel chains planned nearly 2,000 luxury rooms on the Tenderloin's edge. Tenants, seniors and VISTA volunteers answered by rewriting the zoning map.
story: By the late 1970s tourism was booming, and Tenderloin hotel owners worked out that a room renting for $180 a month could fetch $30 or $40 a night [1]. Blocked by rent laws from evicting long-term tenants, some turned down the heat, shut off elevators and pulled the chairs out of lobbies until people left [1]. Then, in summer 1980, Ramada, Hilton and Holiday Inn announced luxury high-rises that together would plant nearly 2,000 rooms on the neighbourhood's eastern edge [1]. The North of Market Planning Coalition, founded in 1978 and staffed by young VISTA organizers, fought back [1]. Joe Kaufman, a disabled poet recently priced out of the Haight, joined after seeing a sign in an Eddy Street laundromat. 'Here was a way to fight back,' he said [1]. Instead of fighting project by project, the coalition drew up its own zoning plan, with fewer bars, limits on commercial uses and height caps of mostly 80 feet, and persuaded the city to adopt most of it [2]. The rezoning became law in 1985. It shut the neighbourhood's core to high-rise development and kept land cheap enough for nonprofits to buy buildings [2][3].

title: Refugees remake a corner as Little Saigon

place.label: Little Saigon, Larkin St between Eddy and O'Farrell

hook: Fleeing war and refugee camps, Southeast Asian families filled Tenderloin studios in the 1980s. Two decades later, the city made their Larkin Street official.
story: From the late 1970s thousands of refugees from Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos arrived in San Francisco, and the Tenderloin's cheap rents made it their main landing place [1]. Suddenly a neighbourhood with no playgrounds and corner stores selling 'lots of liquor but little fresh food' was home to large families squeezed into studios [1]. Community networks helped families open markets selling vegetables, meat and Asian ingredients, followed by dozens of Vietnamese, Chinese and Cambodian restaurants [1]. In September 2003 the Board of Supervisors unanimously named the two blocks of Larkin Street between Eddy and O'Farrell 'Little Saigon' [2]. About 80 percent of the businesses there were Vietnamese American-owned, from Tammy Pham's Kim Cuong Jewelry to Saigon Sandwiches, where Hang Nguyen made about 400 sandwiches a day [2]. 'Not even San Jose, with its large Vietnamese population, has a Little Saigon,' said task force member Phu Nguyen [2]. Green-and-yellow 'Sai Gon Nho' banners went up. In 2008 two pillars topped with marble ky linh, a mythical creature, rose at Larkin and Eddy as a gateway [2][3].

title: The park that was a cage

place.label: Boeddeker Park, 246 Eddy St at Jones

hook: The Tenderloin fought for a park, then got one designed like a fortress, with spiked fences and sprinklers aimed at sleepers. It took three decades to get it right.
story: When refugee families with children poured into the Tenderloin, neighbourhood leaders demanded a park. Boeddeker Park, named for the founder of St. Anthony's Dining Room, opened in 1985 [1]. The Chronicle hoped it would 'welcome elderly bench-sitters and frisky children and shoo away devotees of the twist-off cap' [2]. But the design feared its neighbours: a spiked iron fence, an entrance wide enough for a police car, and sprinklers that came on at odd moments to discourage 'long-term snoozing by the sleeping-bag set' [2]. A decade later a parents' group ranked it last of 45 parks. The Project for Public Spaces called it 'an empty cage watched from outside by drug dealers' [2]. Community meetings began in 2007, and on December 10, 2014, a $9.3 million remake led by the Trust for Public Land reopened [2][3]. It had a lawn, play areas, sloped paths for disabled residents across a 16-foot drop, and a clubhouse by WRNS Studio with a zinc roof rising 31 feet [2]. From 1985 it kept a shade tree and Anthony J. Smith's bronze of 14 residents' faces [2]. About 3,500 children lived within the surrounding 40 blocks [3].

title: A forest grows in Cohen Alley

place.label: Tenderloin National Forest, Cohen Place off Ellis St

hook: An alley full of garbage and syringes became trees, murals, a clay bread oven and a gallery cabin, rented from the city for a dollar.
story: In 1989 Darryl Smith of the Luggage Store, an artists' collective, started paying attention to the dead-end alley beside his building off Ellis Street. He remembered 'garbage…rotting out here, human excrement, syringes' [1]. He and co-director Laurie Lazer saw a place where 'fertile things could happen' [1][2]. Over the next decade they cleaned it, planted trees, vegetables, herbs and flowers, and commissioned murals on every wall [2]. In 2000 they negotiated a lease that closed the alley to traffic for a symbolic $1. The gallery says $1 a year, while a FoundSF essay says $1 a month [1][2]. Artist Kevin Leeper built a sculptured gate. A small green-roofed structure, a wood-fired clay oven and new lighting followed [2]. The alley, officially Cohen Place and about 23 feet wide by 136 feet deep, was renamed the Tenderloin National Forest in May 2009 [2]. The name came from Marco Crescenti, a San Francisco State student [2]. It has hosted concerts, bread-baking and free clothing repair in a neighbourhood with almost no green space [1].

title: Del and Phyllis, first in line

place.label: San Francisco City Hall, 1 Dr Carlton B Goodlett Pl

hook: After more than fifty years together, two lesbian pioneers became the first same-sex couple married at City Hall. Then the courts voided it, and they did it again.
story: On February 12, 2004, Mayor Gavin Newsom ordered city officials to issue marriage licences to same-sex couples. The first couple married were Del Martin and Phyllis Lyon, who had moved in together on Valentine's Day 1953 and co-founded the Daughters of Bilitis, the first lesbian-rights organisation in the country, in 1955 [1][2]. About 4,000 couples followed in the next four weeks, arriving from across the country [3]. At a mass reception for 600 newlyweds on February 23, Lyon said it mattered 'for a lot of the people that got married … but also for our friends who didn't get married' [1]. The state Supreme Court stopped the weddings in March. On August 12, 2004, it declared them void [3]. Four years later the same court struck down California's marriage ban. On June 16, 2008, Martin and Lyon were first in line again, married by Newsom himself in the same mauve and turquoise suits they had worn in 2004 [1][2]. Those outfits are now in the GLBT Historical Society's collection [1]. Martin died that August, aged 87. 'We were able to enjoy the ultimate rite of love and commitment before she passed,' Lyon said [1].

title: From 'seedy' to the National Register

place.label: Central YMCA Hotel, 351 Turk St, in the Uptown Tenderloin Historic District

hook: For decades the papers called it 'seedy'. In 2009 its hotels and apartment blocks became one of the largest residential historic districts in the nation.
story: Almost everything in the Tenderloin was built between the 1906 earthquake and the early 1940s. After the fire, the city required fire-resistant construction, which helps define the district: mostly three- to seven-storey hotels, boarding houses and apartments in Tudor, Spanish Colonial and Renaissance Revival dress, with a few Moderne towers [1]. A survey in 1983 proposed a historic district, but residents rejected it. They feared it would bring gentrification before their protective rezoning was secured [2]. The idea was then forgotten for two decades, until the Tenderloin Housing Clinic won a grant for a new survey in 2006 [2]. On July 25, 2008, the State Historical Resources Commission voted unanimously for the nomination. Its buildings include what Randy Shaw called the world's largest collection of historic single-room-occupancy hotels, plus landmarks like the Central YMCA, the Hibernia Bank and the Alcazar Theater [2]. The Uptown Tenderloin Historic District joined the National Register on February 5, 2009 [1]. Beyond Chron counted 470 buildings, while the Register lists 408 contributing ones [1][2]. Seventy-three plaques now mark buildings across the blocks [1].

title: The tax break that built 'Twitterloin'

place.label: Market Square (former San Francisco Mart), 1355 Market St

hook: Twitter threatened to leave town. San Francisco waived its payroll tax, and a hulking Art Deco furniture mart on a battered stretch of Market became the Twitter Building.
story: In 2011 Mid-Market was reeling. The Great Recession had left about half of its offices and 30 percent of its shops empty [2]. Twitter, then 400 employees and aiming for 3,000, threatened to move to the Peninsula to escape the city's payroll tax [1]. In April 2011 the Board of Supervisors approved a six-year break on payroll taxes for new jobs at companies moving into Central Market and the Tenderloin. Three days later Twitter signed a lease at 1355 Market Street [1]. The building was the 1937 Art Deco San Francisco Mart, more than a million square feet of old furniture showrooms between Ninth and Tenth streets [1][3]. 'The city where we have started and grown will remain our future home,' Twitter's CFO wrote [1]. The company moved in in 2012. Tech firms, restaurants and luxury apartments followed, bringing new fights over displacement and gentrification [2]. The boom did not last. After Elon Musk bought Twitter in 2022 and cut much of its staff, the company, renamed X, put about 460,000 square feet of the building up for sublease in 2024 [4].

title: The world's first transgender district

place.label: Aunt Charlie's Lounge, 133 Turk St, in the Transgender District

hook: Half a century after the Compton's riot, three Black trans women set out to make sure the Tenderloin's trans history, and its trans residents, would not be priced out.
story: By the 2010s, the sound of the Tenderloin was construction noise. New cafes and condos were arriving, and rising rents threatened the transgender community that had long called the neighbourhood home [1]. In 2016 the city renamed parts of Turk and Taylor streets 'Compton's Cafeteria Way' and 'Vikki Mar Lane' [2]. In 2017 three Black trans women founded the Compton's Transgender Cultural District, named for the 1966 riot. It is the first legally recognized transgender district in the world [2]. It covers six blocks of the south-eastern Tenderloin and crosses Market Street to take in two blocks of Sixth Street [2]. Co-founder Honey Mahogany, a drag artist and former contestant on RuPaul's Drag Race, met NPR at Aunt Charlie's Lounge on Turk Street, one of the neighbourhood's few remaining gay bars and, she said, 'a centerpiece for the community' [1]. 'People can't put me in the box of male or female, because I'm tall, because I'm black, or whatever, so I get stared at all over San Francisco,' she told NPR. 'In the Tenderloin I find that doesn't happen' [1]. 'With the destruction of these buildings,' she warned, 'we're also losing the stories that go along with them' [1].
